North York Moors: England's Underrated Motorcycle Playground

The North York Moors National Park sprawls across 554 square miles of open heather moorland, deep wooded valleys, and a dramatically rugged coastline. Sitting between the Vale of York to the west and the North Sea to the east, this is a landscape that delivers big skies, sweeping roads, and a sense of space that surprises riders on their first visit. From August's purple heather bloom to the year-round charm of its stone-built market towns, the Moors reward every mile.

The Moorland Roads

The defining riding experience here is crossing the high moors. The road from Hutton-le-Hole over Blakey Ridge to Castleton runs along one of England's highest open roads, with views that stretch for miles in every direction. In late summer, the heather turns the landscape an extraordinary shade of purple. The A169 from Pickering to Whitby is another classic — a well-surfaced road that climbs onto the moors before descending to the coast through the Hole of Horcum, a massive natural amphitheatre.

The Heritage Coast

The North Yorkshire coast is among England's most dramatic. Whitby, with its ruined gothic abbey and harbourside fish and chip shops, is a must-stop destination. Robin Hood's Bay is a tumbling village of narrow lanes clinging to the cliffside. Staithes, once England's largest fishing port, is a hidden gem reached via a steep lane that rewards you with authentic coastal character.

  • Whitby — Gothic abbey ruins, harbour, Dracula connections, and the Magpie Cafe
  • Robin Hood's Bay — Steep lanes down to a tiny beach, smuggling history
  • Staithes — Unspoiled fishing village where Captain Cook was apprenticed
  • Scarborough — Classic seaside resort, castle headland, excellent fish restaurants

Market Towns and Villages

The Moors' inland villages are full of character. Helmsley is a handsome market town with a ruined castle and the Star Inn at Harome nearby — a Michelin-starred pub. Pickering has a steam railway that runs through the national park to Whitby. Kirkbymoorside and Hutton-le-Hole offer traditional Yorkshire charm without the crowds of the Dales.

The North York Moors in August is one of England's greatest natural spectacles. The heather transforms the landscape into a sea of purple that stretches to the horizon — experience it from two wheels and you'll never forget it.

Best Riding Routes

Beyond the moorland crossings, seek out these roads:

  • Chimney Bank (Rosedale) — One of England's steepest roads at 1-in-3, climbing out of Rosedale Abbey with hairpin bends and a cattle grid at the summit
  • A170 Thirsk to Scarborough — A flowing A-road skirting the southern edge of the moors
  • B1257 Helmsley to Stokesley — Through the Cleveland Hills with open moorland views
  • Coast Road from Whitby to Scarborough — Dramatic clifftop riding via Robin Hood's Bay

Practical Information

The North York Moors are easily accessible — the A1(M) passes to the west and the A64 runs along the southern boundary. York is 40 minutes south, Middlesbrough 30 minutes north. Fuel is available in Pickering, Helmsley, Whitby, and Scarborough, but top up before crossing the moors as there's nothing on the high ground. Accommodation ranges from traditional country pubs to luxury hotels. Best months: May to October, with August being unmissable for the heather. Roads can be affected by fog and ice in winter. Watch for sheep on unfenced moorland roads — they have right of way and absolutely no road sense.
keyTakeaways: The North York Moors cover 554 square miles of heather moorland, wooded valleys and a dramatic coastline between the Vale of York and the North Sea.
The Blakey Ridge crossing and the A169 through the Hole of Horcum are the defining moorland rides.
August's purple heather bloom is one of England's greatest natural spectacles, best experienced from two wheels.
Chimney Bank at Rosedale is one of England's steepest roads at 1-in-3, with hairpins and a summit cattle grid.
Fuel up in Pickering, Helmsley, Whitby or Scarborough before crossing the moors, where there is nothing on the high ground.

faq.q: When is the best time to see the heather on the moors?
faq.a: August is unmissable, when the heather transforms the landscape into a sea of purple stretching to the horizon, one of England's greatest natural spectacles. The wider best season runs May to October. Roads can be affected by fog and ice in winter, so the warmer months offer the safest and most rewarding riding.

faq.q: What is the most dramatic road in the North York Moors?
faq.a: Chimney Bank at Rosedale is one of England's steepest roads at 1-in-3, climbing out of Rosedale Abbey with hairpin bends and a cattle grid at the summit. For a classic moorland crossing, the road from Hutton-le-Hole over Blakey Ridge to Castleton runs along one of England's highest open roads with vast views.

faq.q: Where should I refuel when crossing the moors?
faq.a: Fuel is available in Pickering, Helmsley, Whitby and Scarborough, but top up before crossing the moors as there is nothing on the high ground. The open moorland roads can be exposed and remote, so it is wise to start any crossing with a full tank rather than risk running low miles from the nearest town.

faq.q: Which coastal villages are worth visiting?
faq.a: Whitby, with its ruined gothic abbey, harbourside fish and chip shops and Dracula connections, is a must-stop. Robin Hood's Bay tumbles down steep lanes to a tiny beach with a smuggling history, and Staithes is an unspoiled fishing village where Captain Cook was apprenticed. Scarborough offers a classic seaside resort with a castle headland.

faq.q: How accessible are the North York Moors?
faq.a: The moors are easily reached, with the A1(M) passing to the west and the A64 running along the southern boundary. York is 40 minutes to the south and Middlesbrough 30 minutes to the north. Watch for sheep on unfenced moorland roads, as they have right of way and no road sense whatsoever.
